chunk_findings.detail: The wait loop sleeps `min(poll, left)` and only calls `renew()` after that sleep; it never bounds the sleep by the lease heartbeat interval. If a caller has a lease whose `[lease].heartbeat_s` is 60 and invokes `watch(file=..., until=..., heartbeat="item", poll_s=300)` (or any `poll_s` larger than the heartbeat), the call sleeps until the bounded wait deadline and renews only at the end, so the lease expires after 60 seconds and can be taken by another holder. The throttled pacer cannot help because its callable is not invoked during the sleep, defeating the stated purpose of renewing leases while waiting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/watch.py:watch

chunk_findings.detail: `_target` rejects a token combined with `job`, `file`, `pid`, or `gate`, but silently ignores `until` and `heartbeat`. Given a valid file watch token whose encoded `until` is `r"OLD"`, calling `watch(token= [REDACTED] until=r"NEW")` uses the decoded token target and matches `OLD`, not the requested `NEW`. Similarly, `watch(token= [REDACTED] heartbeat="new-item")` ignores `new-item` and renews only the leases encoded in the token, so the caller’s newly requested lease can expire. The token should either be accepted alone with all conflicting facets rejected, or the extra `until`/`heartbeat` values should be applied.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/watch.py:_target

chunk_findings.detail: `decode` promises to return `None` for any token that is not a watch token, but it only catches `ValueError` and `TypeError`. A valid base64 token whose JSON decodes to a non-object reaches `d.items()` and raises `AttributeError`; for example, `decode("W10")` (base64url for `[]`) crashes instead of returning `None`. If a caller passes a resume token from user input or MCP, this can become an unhandled crash rather than a clean “not a token” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:55

chunk_findings.detail: `problem` does not reject `until` unless `file` is set. It checks `t.file and not t.until`, but never checks `t.until and not t.file`, so `Target(job="1", until="x")` passes validation, as does a target with `pid` or `gate` plus `until`. If the CLI/API allows `--until` with `--job`, `--pid`, or `--gate`, the target kind is the non-file target and the regex is silently ignored, contrary to the stated requirement that `--until` belongs only with `--file`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:62

chunk_findings.detail: The file rewrite detection resets only when the current size is strictly smaller than the stored offset. If a watched file is truncated and rewritten to the same or larger size before the next scan, the offset is not reset and the beginning of the new file is skipped. For example, after a prior scan leaves `t.offset=10`, if the file is replaced by the 10-byte content `b"PASS\nFAIL\n"`, `len(data) < t.offset` is false, `pos` starts at 10, and `scan_file` returns `None` even though `PASS` is on the first line of the rewritten file.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:90

chunk_findings.detail: `_text` drops the resume token on the timeout path. A bounded watch that has not completed is represented by `out.exit == 2` and the resumable token is carried in `out.data["token"]`, but `if out.exit:` returns only `out.reason`. For example, `ddflow watch --file ci.out --until DONE --timeout 1` with no matching line yet reaches this branch and the rendered text contains only the timeout reason, not the token required by the command's own description ("exit 2 ... carries a `token`") to resume the same watch. The token is printed only when `out.exit` is falsey, i.e. when the watch has already completed and no resume is needed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/watch.py:18

chunk_findings.detail: The new `ddflow_watch` tool is wired as a top-level `watch` command in the API layer (`test_api_layer.py` maps `ddflow_watch` to the CLI shape `["watch", "--pid", ...]`), but the MCP alias table maps the same tool name to `ddflow_lease action=watch`. Because the alias table is the MCP routing contract, an MCP call to `ddflow_watch` with watch arguments such as `{"pid": 123}` (or `{"file": "ci.out", "until": "DONE"}`) is dispatched to the `lease` family/action rather than to the new `watch` surface/service. The lease action schema does not accept the new `--job`, `--file`, `--until`, or `--gate` options, so valid watch requests are rejected or routed to the wrong implementation, bypassing the resumable-token watch logic introduced by this change.
chunk_findings.title: tests/data/mcp_tool_aliases.json:"ddflow_watch"

chunk_findings.detail: The monkeypatched `throttled` returns a callable whose return value is the tuple `(None, renew())` rather than the result of `renew()`. If the watcher uses the return value of the throttled renewal callback to decide whether to record an item in `unrenewed`, a failed renewal (`renew()` returning false) will still be treated as successful because the tuple is truthy; the test can therefore pass with `out.data["unrenewed"] == []` even though the named lease was not actually renewed. The stub should preserve the renewal result, e.g. by using a nested function that appends and then returns `renew()`, or by returning `(calls.append(1), renew())[1]`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_watch.py:102

chunk_findings.detail: `_probe` treats every job state that is not exactly `"running"` as terminal. `_refuse_elsewhere` explicitly says an `"elsewhere"` job cannot be watched from this host, but `_probe` does not check for it: after a reload, if `J.status(job).state` becomes `"elsewhere"` (for example, another host claims the job after the watch started), `_probe` returns `{"status": "elsewhere", ...}`, so `watch` returns `O.ok` with `matched: True` and exit 0. The job has not finished and is not watchable; the returned token then behaves differently on resume because `_refuse_elsewhere` will return `O.nothing`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/watch.py:_probe (job branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The loop sleeps before the first lease renewal. Given a caller whose lease is close to expiry, `watch(repo, job="J", timeout_s=300, poll_s=5)` can let the lease lapse before it is renewed: `_probe` returns `None`, `left` is about 300 seconds, the code sleeps `min(5, left, heartbeat_s/2)` (up to 5 seconds here), and only then calls `renew()`. If the lease expires in one second, it expires during the first sleep. The renewal should happen after `_load`/before the first sleep, not after it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/watch.py:watch (sleep before first `renew`)

chunk_findings.detail: `timeout_s=float("nan")` passes the validation at lines 130-132 because `nan < 0` and `nan > WAIT_MAX_S` are both false. The deadline becomes `NaN`, `left` is `NaN`, `left <= 0` is never true, and the loop never times out. Likewise, `poll_s=float("nan")` passes `poll <= 0` and reaches `time.sleep(...)`, which raises `ValueError`. Non-finite timeout/poll values should be rejected as invalid arguments.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/watch.py:watch (NaN timeout/poll validation)

chunk_findings.detail: `decode` promises to return `None` when a token is not one of ours, but it does not catch `binascii.Error`. A truncated or corrupt resumable token such as `"a"` is padded to `"a==="`, and `base64.urlsafe_b64decode` raises `binascii.Error` for invalid base64/padding. Because that exception is not included in `except (ValueError, TypeError, AttributeError)`, the function propagates it instead of returning `None`, so a malformed caller-supplied token can crash the watch API’s token-resume path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:52

chunk_findings.detail: `scan_file`’s rewrite detection only resets the saved offset when the file is shorter than the offset or when the first 64 bytes differ. If a watched file is rewritten/truncated and re-appended between polls so that its size is at least the saved offset and its first 64 bytes are unchanged (for example, the same log header), the stale offset is used. Given a token with `offset=1000` and `sig` matching the old first 64 bytes, if `ci.out` is recreated with the same 64-byte header, length 1200, and a matching `FAIL` line before byte 1000, `scan_file` starts at 1000 and skips that line (and can even return a fragment if line boundaries moved), so the watch never sees the event.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:100

chunk_findings.detail: The new `watch` command is a poll-wait/hold primitive: it tells agents to wait for a job/file/pid/gate, exposes `poll` (default 2) and `timeout`, and renews leases while waiting. For example, an agent running `ddflow watch --job 123 --poll 2` blocks and polls every two seconds until the job exits, which is the pattern [r-lock-cycle-selfheal] says agents must not use; the project is supposed to resolve waits by adding needs edges rather than by waiting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/watch.py:COMMANDS

chunk_findings.detail: The change treats `ddflow_watch` as a hot single by adding it to the same small frozenset that already contains `ddflow_review`, `ddflow_verify`, and `ddflow_wait`—the hot-single set used by `tests/test_mcp_aliases.py` as `F.HOT_SINGLES`—while also adding `ddflow_watch` to the MCP alias table and raising the expected alias count to 113. Those two states are mutually exclusive: `test_one_alias_per_old_name_that_is_not_a_hot_single` asserts `set(A.ALIASES) == set(TOOLS) - set(F.HOT_SINGLES) - own`. Given this change, `ddflow_watch` is both present in the alias data/actual alias registry and subtracted by `HOT_SINGLES`; running that test fails either because the set equality includes/excludes `ddflow_watch` inconsistently, or because the actual hot-single-aware alias count remains 112 while the test now asserts 113.

chunk_findings.detail: `_refuse_elsewhere` is only called before the wait loop, but the changed job probe now treats `state == "elsewhere"` as “not finished” by returning `None`. If a job that was initially watchable becomes `elsewhere` during the wait—for example, the caller’s lease lapses and another host claims the job—the loop reloads state, `_probe` returns `None`, and the code continues sleeping until the timeout and returns a timed-out token. Given `watch(job="123", timeout=120)` where the job record changes to `elsewhere` after 10 seconds, the call should return the “cannot be watched from here” refusal, but it instead returns exit 2 timed out with a token that will be rejected on resume.

chunk_findings.detail: The added reassignment `renew, missed = _pacer(log, cfg, st, t.heartbeat)` inside the reload branch discards whatever missed-renewal collection was returned by the previous pacer. If a heartbeat renewal fails before a job/gate reload occurs, and then the folded-log mark changes or `RECHECK_S` elapses causing `_load` and a fresh `_pacer`, the final `unrenewed` data derived from `missed` can be empty even though the named lease was not renewed. For example, `watch(job="1", heartbeat="item", timeout=60)` where the first `renew()` fails and then `RECHECK_S` elapses before timeout can report `unrenewed: []`, hiding a lease-renewal failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/watch.py:renew, missed = _pacer

chunk_findings.detail: The token validator added in this diff checks that `offset` is an `int`, but it does not reject negative offsets. A resume token whose decoded JSON is `{"file":"ci.out","until":"DONE","offset":-1}` passes the new type checks and is then accepted by `problem()` because `file`+`until` is otherwise a valid target. `offset` is documented as “bytes already read”, so `-1` is not a valid byte position; the file watcher uses it as a start index. For example, if `ci.out` already contains `b"DONE\n"`, resuming with this token makes the scan start at `-1`, which under Python bytes slicing/seek semantics does not mean “from the start” and can read only the trailing byte rather than the whole file, so the matching `DONE` line can be missed even though it was present. Since tokens may be supplied by a caller/MCP rather than generated internally, `decode` should return `None` for this invalid token instead of accepting an impossible resume state.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:decode

chunk_findings.detail: The new rewrite check compares only a 64-byte prefix digest and the length against the stored offset, so a replacement that preserves those 64 bytes and is not shorter than the old offset is treated as an append and the stale offset is used as a line boundary. For example, after scanning a file whose first complete line ends at byte 100, `t.offset=100` and `t.sig` is the digest of the first 64 bytes. Replace the file with the same first 64 bytes, then 36 bytes of `N`, then `DONE\n` (total length >= 100). The next `scan_file` sees `len(data) >= 100` and the same signature, does not reset, starts at byte 100 inside the line that begins at byte 64, and with `until=r"^DONE"` returns the suffix `DONE` even though no complete line in the new file matches; if the new length is exactly 100 and a matching line lies entirely before byte 100, it returns `None` and misses it. Thus the signature fix still allows header-preserving rewrites to produce wrong or missed results.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/watch.py:scan_file

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertions `_watch(proj, pid=4, timeout_s=float("nan")).exit == 1` and `_watch(proj, pid=4, until="x").exit == 1` use an arbitrary PID as the target, and the `until` assertion has no timeout. In a container where PID 4 is absent, both calls can return exit 1 from the missing-process path, so the assertions pass even if NaN timeouts or `until` with a non-file target are not actually rejected. Conversely, on a Linux host where PID 4 exists, if `until` with `--pid` is still ignored, the call has no timeout and waits for a kernel thread that never exits, so the regression test hangs instead of failing. The test therefore does not reliably verify the claimed facet-validation fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_watch.py:test_a_token_with_extra_facets_or_junk_is_refused

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite detection still misses a rewritten file that keeps the first 64 bytes and is not shorter than the saved offset; the change only adds a docstring describing the limitation. Given a resumable file token with `offset=1000` and `sig` equal to the first 64-byte header, replace the watched file with a new file that has the same first 64 bytes, total length 1200, and a matching line at byte 100. `scan_file` reads the whole file, sees `len(data) >= offset` and the same header digest, so it starts scanning at byte 1000 and never inspects the new matching line, returning no match. This is still a wrong result: `scan_file` already has the whole file in memory and could distinguish this rewrite from an append (for example by comparing a digest of the prefix up to the saved offset, or by using inode/mtime metadata), so documenting the case as indistinguishable does not answer the previously confirmed defect.
